summary: Describes how to measure the time a link-state routing protocol such as IS-IS or OSPF takes to converge after a change. The tests use outside, black-box observations of data-plane traffic. It builds on the terminology in RFC 6412 and is informational.

eli5.summary: When a bridge closes, how long until every car takes the detour? This gives the recipe for timing that with routers, so different testers get comparable results.

questions: how to measure ospf convergence time
what is route loss of connectivity period
subtitle: A black-box recipe for timing how long a router takes to reroute traffic after a link-state IGP change.

tldr.problem: Operators and vendors need comparable numbers for how fast IS-IS or OSPF routers converge, but internal timers differ by architecture, so measuring them directly is not comparable.
tldr.mechanism: A Tester emulates neighbor routers, sends traffic through the Device Under Test, triggers a Convergence Event such as a link failure, and derives convergence times from packet loss and forwarding rate on the data plane.
tldr.outcome: It defines test topologies, measurement methods, a reporting format and ten test cases. Terms come from RFC 6412.

today: RFC 6413 is an Informational document and the metadata shows no obsoleting or updating RFC. Its terms are defined in RFC 6412.

sections.title: Why Measure on the Data Plane
sections.content:
Service providers use IGP convergence time as a key metric of router design, and their customers judge service by the packet loss it causes. So the RFC measures convergence by packet loss and other impairments, which are externally observable events with direct impact on applications. Measuring on the data plane accounts for all factors in convergence time and needs no knowledge of the router's internals.

It lists four categories of factors: event detection, SPF processing, LSA/LSP advertisement and FIB update, plus increased forwarding delay from queueing. Their contribution varies with each vendor's architecture, which is why a black-box test is useful for comparing routers.

The scope covers IPv4 and IPv6 and link-state IGPs such as IS-IS and OSPF. Adjacencies over tunnels, non-point-to-point adjacencies, BFD, NSF, NSR, Graceful Restart and fast reroute mechanisms are out of scope.
sections.eli5: You can time a detour by watching how long cars are stuck, without opening the traffic computer. That works for any brand of router.

sections.title: Test Topologies
sections.content:
In every topology a Tester emulates neighbor routers and IGP adjacencies must be established between it and the DUT. For local changes, the Tester emulates three routers: RTa on the Ingress Interface, RTb on the Preferred Egress Interface and RTc on the Next-Best Egress Interface. A variant makes the Next-Best Egress Interfaces an ECMP set with N routers, for N+2 in total.

For remote changes, two routers DUT1 and DUT2 form the System Under Test and should be identically configured devices of the same model. A packet-forwarding loop (micro-loop) may occur briefly between them during convergence. Further topologies cover a local ECMP set, a remote ECMP set and a parallel link set.
sections.eli5: The test machine pretends to be several neighboring routers. One sends traffic in, one is the main road out and one is the detour.

sections.title: Convergence Time and Loss of Connectivity
sections.content:
Route Convergence time runs from the Convergence Event Instant until the DUT is ready to forward traffic for a route on the Next-Best Egress Interface and keeps doing so for the Sustained Convergence Validation Time. The Route Loss of Connectivity Period is the time traffic to that route is lost. The latter is the one with direct impact on users, and it is expected to be a single Loss Period.

Generally convergence time is larger than or equal to the loss period. They are equal if the event causes instantaneous traffic loss, such as a fiber cut on the Preferred Egress Interface.

For events without instant loss, such as a reversion of a link failure, the Tester observes only the Next-Best Egress Interface. A loss-derived method then needs the time between the Start Traffic Instant and the Convergence Event Instant subtracted. The RFC shows convergence time as the Next-Best Egress Interface loss period minus that gap. It also shows with sample numbers (Ta=0, Tb=1, Ta'=3, Tb'=5) why global statistics can overstate the loss period range, which is why the route-specific method is preferred.
sections.eli5: Some drivers are stuck for a short time and some for longer. If you only look at the whole crowd, you get the range wrong, so you follow individual drivers.

sections.title: Test Considerations and Reporting
sections.content:
Test conditions affect results. IGP convergence SHOULD be benchmarked without routes from other protocols. The Tester emulates a single IGP topology, and the number of routes and nodes should approximate the real network, for example thousands of routes with tens or hundreds of nodes. Timers such as the hello timer and LSA/LSP generation delay should be set as in the operational network.

The Offered Load SHOULD be the minimum of the measured Throughput over the primary and backup path. Packet size is selectable and MUST be recorded. Destination addresses MUST spread over all routes or a statistically representative subset, and the load should be randomly distributed across header fields so ECMP hashing is exercised. Its duration MUST be longer than the convergence time plus the Sustained Convergence Validation Time. Results vary between trials, so a small number of trials needs care.

The reporting format asks for the test case, topology figure, IGP, interface type, packet size, offered load, number of routes, sampling interval and timer values, then the loss counts and each benchmark in seconds, including minimum, maximum, median and average route-specific times.
sections.eli5: To make a fair test, use realistic amounts of traffic, spread it over all destinations, repeat it, and write down every setting you used.

sections.title: The Test Cases
sections.content:
Every test case follows one generic procedure: set up the DUT and Tester and advertise an IGP topology, send Offered Load, verify traffic is forwarded without Impaired Packets, introduce the Convergence Event, measure First Route and Full Convergence Time, stop the load, compute the route-specific and loss-derived values, wait for queues to drain, then restart the load and repeat for the reversed event.

The cases cover interface failure and recovery (local, remote, ECMP member local, ECMP member remote and parallel link member), other failures (Layer 2 session loss and loss of an IGP adjacency), route withdrawal and re-advertisement, administrative disabling of a local interface, and cost change. For Layer 2 and adjacency tests, the other layer must be kept up and timers set so it does not time out first.
sections.eli5: Each test breaks one thing, such as a cable, a setting or a price on a road, times the recovery, then puts it back and times that too.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Tests are limited to controlled laboratory stimuli with dedicated address space. The benchmarking topology MUST be independent and MUST NOT be connected to devices that could forward test traffic into a production network or misroute it to the management network. The DUT SHOULD NOT have special benchmarking capabilities, so its security implications match production.
sections.eli5: Do the experiment in a sealed test lab so practice traffic cannot spill onto real networks.
